stages.name: Integration
stages.title: Trade blocs and monetary union
stages.sub: How countries move from cutting tariffs between themselves to sharing one currency, and what that final step needs to work.

steps.q: France sells cheese to Germany. Germany charges an extra amount on it at the border, on top of the price, purely because it crossed a border. What kind of charge is that?
steps.right: A border tax on an import
steps.wrong: A subsidy paid to the seller
steps.hint: It is added only because the good came from another country.

steps.q: Three countries agree to scrap tariffs on goods traded between themselves, but each still sets its own tariff on goods coming in from outside countries. What has just been formed between them?
steps.right: A group with free trade only among its own members
steps.wrong: A group with one shared tariff on all outsiders
steps.hint: Look at what changed only for trade between the members, not with the rest of the world.

steps.q: Now those same countries go further: they agree that any good entering from outside the group faces the same tariff, whichever member country it arrives in. What has this stopped a trader doing?
steps.right: Bringing goods in via the member with the lowest tariff
steps.hint: Before this, could a trader pick the cheapest entry point into the group?

steps.q: The group now also lets workers, businesses and money move and set up freely in any member country, with no special permission needed. What has been removed?
steps.right: Barriers to factors of production moving between members
steps.wrong: Barriers to goods moving between members only
steps.hint: Workers and capital are factors of production, not goods. What has changed for them?

steps.q: Members now go further still and scrap their own currencies, adopting one shared currency for all of them, set by one central bank. What can no member now do on its own?
steps.right: Set its own exchange rate or interest rate
steps.wrong: Trade goods with non-members at all
steps.hint: Interest rates and the exchange rate used to be set separately by each country. Who sets them now?

steps.q: Greece and Germany share the euro but have very different economies. If Greece suffers a downturn while Germany booms, Greece cannot cut its own interest rate or devalue its own currency to help. What does this suggest members need for the shared currency to work well?
steps.hint: One interest rate is set for everyone. Does that work better if economies move together or move very differently?
